title: Averages & Mixtures
weightage: High — averages appear across statistics, Data Interpretation and word problems; alligation is a fast bonus tool
intro: An average is nothing more than a fair-share redistribution: total ÷ count. That one definition — read backwards as total = average × count — solves the large majority of GRE average questions, because the test almost always gives you two of the three quantities and asks for the third. The wrinkle the GRE leans on is the weighted average: when groups have different sizes, the combined average is pulled toward the bigger group, never the plain midpoint of the two averages. Mixtures are weighted averages in disguise (blend two salt solutions and the result’s concentration is the weighted average of the two), and alligation is a lightning-fast shortcut for finding the ratio in which to mix them. The last piece is "change in average" — how one new value or one swap shifts the mean — which the GRE tests constantly because it rewards understanding over grinding. This chapter builds all four: the arithmetic mean, weighted averages, mixtures and alligation, and change-in-average reasoning.

topics.name: Arithmetic Mean
topics.details: The arithmetic mean is the sum of the values divided by how many there are. The most useful reframing for the GRE is the reverse: sum = average × count. If six numbers average 15, their total is 90 — and now any question about one missing value, or about what happens when you add a seventh number, becomes simple. A second powerful idea is the deviation view: the mean is the balance point where the amounts above it exactly cancel the amounts below it, so if most values are clustered you can guess-and-adjust from a convenient anchor. For evenly spaced sets (consecutive integers, arithmetic sequences), the mean is just the average of the first and last terms, so the mean of 1 through 99 is (1 + 99)/2 = 50 without any summing. Keep the count honest — "the average of the integers from 1 to 10 inclusive" has 10 terms, not 9.

topics.name: Weighted Average
topics.details: When the groups being combined are different sizes, you cannot just average the averages — you must weight each average by its group size: combined = (n₁a₁ + n₂a₂)/(n₁ + n₂). A class of 30 averaging 70 combined with a class of 10 averaging 90 does not average 80; it averages (30·70 + 10·90)/40 = (2100 + 900)/40 = 75, pulled toward the bigger (lower-scoring) group. The key intuition — and a frequent Quantitative Comparison hook — is that the weighted mean always lands between the two averages, closer to the group with more weight. This same structure appears everywhere on the GRE: GPA (grades weighted by credit hours), average speed (speeds weighted by time), portfolio returns, and blended prices. Whenever a problem gives you two averages and two different counts, reach for the weighted formula, not the plain midpoint.

solved.problem: A class of 30 averages 70; a class of 10 averages 90. Combined average?
A student scores 80 on a test worth 40% and 90 on one worth 60%. Weighted average?
Quantitative Comparison. Group X (20 people) averages 50; group Y (5 people) averages 80. Quantity A: the combined average. Quantity B: 65. Which is greater?
solved.solution: Combined = (20·50 + 5·80)/25 = (1000 + 400)/25 = 1400/25 = 56. Quantity B (65) is greater — the average leans toward the larger group X.

topics.name: Mixtures & Alligation
topics.details: A mixture problem blends two ingredients of known "strength" (price, concentration, purity) and asks about the result — or, run in reverse, asks in what ratio to blend them to hit a target. Because the blend’s strength is the weighted average of the parts, alligation gives the ratio in one line: the amounts are in the ratio of the cross differences, n₁ : n₂ = (a₂ − M) : (M − a₁), where M is the target and a₁ < M < a₂. To make a 40%-milk blend from 20% and 50% milks, the ratio is (50 − 40) : (40 − 20) = 10 : 20 = 1 : 2, so use twice as much of the weaker one. Alligation is the GRE-fast route for "how many litres of water to add", "what ratio of two coffees", and profit questions dressed as tea blends. A close cousin is repeated replacement — draw off some mixture and top up with pure solvent — where the remaining original follows original × (1 − r/V)ⁿ after n rounds.

solved.problem: In what ratio should 20% and 50% salt solutions be mixed to get 30%?
How much water must be added to 10 litres of 40% acid to dilute it to 25%?
solved.solution: Acid stays fixed at 4 L. Need 4 = 25% of total ⇒ total = 16 L, so add 16 − 10 = 6 litres.

solved.problem: Coffee at $8/kg is mixed with coffee at $14/kg to sell at $10/kg. Find the mixing ratio.

topics.name: Change-in-Average Problems
topics.details: These questions ask how the mean shifts when you add a value, remove one, or swap one out — and the fast way is to track the total, not to recompute the whole average. Adding a new value that is above the current average pulls the mean up; below it, down; equal to it, no change. The size of the shift is governed by how far the new value sits from the old mean, spread across the new count. A cleaner tool for "one value replaced by another" is to work with the change in sum: if a value goes up by 12 across a set of 6, the average rises by 12/6 = 2. The GRE’s classic version is the cricket-or-batting-average style: "a player averaging 40 over 10 innings scores 84 in the 11th — new average?" — total goes from 400 to 484 over 11 innings, giving 44. Always convert the average condition into a statement about the total first; the rest is one subtraction and one division.

solved.problem: A student averages 72 over 4 tests. What must she score on a 5th test to raise the average to 75?
solved.solution: Needed total = 75 × 5 = 375. Current total = 72 × 4 = 288. Fifth score = 375 − 288 = 87.

solved.problem: The average of 10 numbers is 30. If one number, 18, is removed, what is the new average?
solved.solution: Total = 300; remove 18 → 282 over 9 numbers. New average = 282/9 = 31.33… ≈ 31.3.

solved.problem: A player averages 40 over 10 innings, then scores 84 in the 11th. New average?
In a set of 6 numbers averaging 25, one value is increased by 30. By how much does the average rise?
solved.solution: The sum rises 30, spread over 6 numbers: 30/6 = 5, so the average rises by 5 (to 30).

shortcuts: Rewrite every average condition as a total: total = average × count. Two of the three are always given.
For evenly spaced sets, the mean is just (first + last)/2 — no summing needed (1 to 99 averages 50).
A weighted average always lands between the two averages, closer to the group with more weight — a fast Quantitative Comparison cue.
Alligation gives the mixing ratio in one line: n₁ : n₂ = (a₂ − M) : (M − a₁), the cross differences around the target M.
To change an average, track the change in the SUM: raising one value by d over n items lifts the mean by d/n.
Diluting with water keeps the pure component fixed — solve from that constant amount, not the changing total.
mistakes: Averaging two group averages directly when the groups are different sizes (ignoring the weights).
Miscounting an inclusive range — 20 to 40 inclusive has 21 terms, not 20.
In alligation, mixing up which difference belongs to which ingredient (pair each amount with the OTHER’s gap).
Recomputing an entire average from scratch instead of adjusting the total for a change-in-average question.
Forgetting that adding a value equal to the current mean leaves the average unchanged.
In dilution, changing the amount of the pure component — only the total (with added water) changes.

pyq.q: Quantitative Comparison — class A (40 students) averages 60; class B (10 students) averages 90. Quantity A: combined average. Quantity B: 70. Which is greater?
pyq.a: Combined = (40·60 + 10·90)/50 = (2400 + 900)/50 = 66. Quantity B (70) is greater — the mean leans toward the larger class A.

pyq.q: Change in average — 6 numbers average 15. Adding a 7th makes the average 16. What is the 7th number?
Numeric Entry — in what ratio must 10% and 40% solutions be mixed to get 30%? Enter as weaker : stronger.
Mixture — 8 litres of 25% acid are mixed with 2 litres of 75% acid. What is the concentration?

summary: Every average question collapses into total = average × count, so convert the words into a statement about the total and the rest is arithmetic. When groups differ in size, use the weighted average — it always sits between the two averages and closer to the larger group, which alone settles many Quantitative Comparisons. Mixtures are weighted averages, and alligation reads off the mixing ratio in one line from the cross differences around the target. For change-in-average problems, track the change in the sum rather than recomputing, and in dilution remember the pure component stays constant while only the total moves. Master these four and you cover a wide band of GRE arithmetic, statistics and Data Interpretation.
